summary:
OrbitCraft is an interactive 3D game where players design and launch a complete space mission, step by step. They choose a mission goal and scientific instruments, build a spacecraft from real subsystems like solar panels, batteries, antennas and propulsion, then select a rocket and an orbit. Throughout the game, live readouts track mass, budget, power and fuel, so every choice has a visible consequence.

The challenge asks for a game that shows how mission design trade-offs connect. OrbitCraft does this by turning one mission into a single connected experience, from idea to verdict. When something goes wrong, the game explains why, for example when an antenna cannot reach the Moon, and suggests a fix. Players can then redesign and try again.

This matters because students rarely get to experience the whole mission process. OrbitCraft makes space engineering understandable, hands-on, and encouraging. Failure becomes the lesson, and learners build the confidence to try again.
details:
What it does and how it works

OrbitCraft takes a player through one complete space mission in four connected phases. First, they pick a mission objective (such as Lunar Polar Exploration) and scientific instruments. Second, they assemble a 3D spacecraft from subsystems: structure, solar panels, batteries, propulsion, antenna, avionics, thermal, shielding, attitude control and instruments. Third, they choose a launch vehicle and orbit, check payload mass and delta-v margins, and watch the 3D launch. Fourth, they see the mission result with a score breakdown and engineering feedback.

Live readouts for mass, budget, power and onboard delta-v update as the player changes the design. If something is wrong, the game explains why (for example, an antenna that cannot reach the Moon) and offers a fix.

Benefits

Players see how each choice affects the others instead of studying topics separately. The game uses simple explanations, hints and visual indicators, so no prior knowledge is needed. Failure is safe, informative and repeatable.

Intended impact

We want students to understand real mission trade-offs by doing, and to treat failure as part of learning. Our design takes inspiration from a quote shared at this hackathon: “Difficulties are just things to overcome after all.” As next steps, we plan to reach more learners, including students, teachers and museums, and to find a way to sustain the project. Those parts are not built yet, because this hackathon focused on implementation.

Tools and technologies

  • JavaScript, with Three.js for 3D rendering and GLB spacecraft models
  • Vite for development and bundling
  • Docker (node:24-alpine) for an identical environment on every team computer
  • GitHub for branches and pull requests
  • Vercel for deployment
  • NASA 3D resources as a reference for spacecraft assets

What is creative about it

OrbitCraft combines the whole mission in one playable experience, where most tools cover one topic. The mission-control interface, the 3D hangar with the spacecraft and rocket, and the warnings with one-click auto-fix make engineering feel like a game. The game teaches through consequences, not through pass or fail.

Factors we considered

  • Accessibility: making it understandable for beginners
  • Realism vs. simplicity: keeping the physics simplified but faithful, with real constraints like payload capacity and delta-v
  • Feedback: explaining why a decision works or fails
  • Teamwork: splitting the work into four modules with shared data formats and a central game state, so we could build in parallel
  • Time: delivering a working end-to-end mission within the hackathon
